definition: A measure put in place to reduce risk to systems, data, people or buildings.
How a control is implemented: technical, managerial, operational or physical.
What a control does about an incident: preventive, deterrent, detective, corrective, compensating or directive.
A control implemented by hardware, software or firmware, such as a firewall rule, encryption or antivirus.
A control based on management's oversight of risk, such as a risk assessment, a security policy or a supplier review.
A control carried out by people as part of day-to-day work, such as security awareness training.
A tangible barrier or device that protects buildings and equipment, such as a lock, fence or bollard.
A control that stops an unwanted action from succeeding, such as a firewall rule or a door lock.
A control that discourages an attempt, for example by warning of consequences or of being caught, without blocking it.
A control that identifies and reports an incident during or after it, without stopping it, such as an IDS alert or a log review.
A control that repairs damage and restores normal operation after an incident, such as restoring files from backup.
An approved alternative used when a required control cannot be implemented. It reduces the same risk to a similar level.
A control that tells people what they must or must not do, such as a policy, procedure or instruction sign.
An intrusion detection system only alerts, so it is detective. An intrusion prevention system blocks the traffic, so it is preventive.
